METADATA.title: Vintage Gibson SG Standard Value Guide: Prices By Year
METADATA.description: SG Standard values from $2,400 to $25,000 by year through 1979. Joe explains small guards, lyre Vibrolas, original humbuckers and repaired necks.
METADATA.h1: Vintage Gibson SG Standard Value Guide

OUTLINE: ## Gibson SG Standard Values By Year
## Early Standards: Pickups And The Factory Vibrato
## Questions About Gibson SG Standard Value
BODY:
Vintage Gibson SG Standard reference values run from $2,400 to $3,000 for typical 1970s cherry guitars to $13,500 to $25,000 for early small-guard examples, as of October 2026. Original humbuckers, the factory vibrato and an unbroken neck put the strongest examples near the top of their group.

For the year and original specification, use my [Gibson SG Standard dating and identification guide](/gibson-sg-dating-guide/#sg-standard). This guide covers market value and the features that move it.

## Gibson SG Standard Values By Year

**Reviewed October 2026. US dollars.** Repeated numbers are shared era references, not separate measurements for each year. Read the condition notes with the table.

| Year | Value Range | Configuration And Year Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1961 | $13,500 to $25,000 | Small guard, early humbuckers and sideways vibrato. |
| 1962 | $13,500 to $25,000 | Small guard, early humbuckers and sideways vibrato. |
| 1963 | $13,500 to $25,000 | Small guard; long lyre Vibrola becomes familiar. |
| 1964 | $13,500 to $25,000 | Small guard; long lyre Vibrola becomes familiar. |
| 1965 | $12,000 to $14,000 | Nut-width and plating transition; small guard. |
| 1966 | $5,000 to $8,000 | Small to large guard transition; match actual version. |
| 1967 | $5,000 to $8,000 | Large guard, full-size humbuckers and lyre Vibrola. |
| 1968 | $5,000 to $8,000 | Large guard, full-size humbuckers and lyre Vibrola. |
| 1969 | $5,000 to $8,000 | Large guard, full-size humbuckers and lyre Vibrola. |
| 1970 | $5,000 to $8,000 | Large guard, full-size humbuckers and lyre Vibrola. |
| 1971 | $5,000 to $8,000 | Large-guard Standard only; SG Deluxe excluded. |
| 1972 | $2,400 to $3,000 | Standard returns; identify it separately from Deluxe. |
| 1973 | $2,400 to $3,000 | Small guard, block inlays and later bridge configurations. |
| 1974 | $2,400 to $3,000 | Small guard, block inlays and later bridge configurations. |
| 1975 | $2,400 to $3,000 | Small guard, block inlays and later bridge configurations. |
| 1976 | $2,400 to $3,000 | Small guard, block inlays and later bridge configurations. |
| 1977 | $2,400 to $3,000 | Small guard, block inlays and later bridge configurations. |
| 1978 | $2,400 to $3,000 | Small guard, block inlays and later bridge configurations. |
| 1979 | $2,400 to $3,000 | Small guard, block inlays and later bridge configurations. |

The 1966 large-guard reference applies after the redesign; an early small-guard guitar needs the preceding configuration considered. The later 1960s source group includes cherry and walnut, so it is not a cherry-only estimate. The 1971 row excludes the SG Deluxe, and 1972 applies to the returning Standard. The 1970s range is cherry only; other catalog finishes are excluded from that particular band.

### Condition Behind The Ranges

**1961 To 1964 Small-Guard Standard:** Original cherry finish and vintage original pickups, no disclosed structural repair, original case. Very Good to Excellent. Minor binding maintenance, a damaged knob or missing pickup decal can be present. Factory vibrato versions included.

**1965 SG Standard, Cherry, Small Guard And Maestro:** Clean, all-original examples with original case and no structural repairs; normal light wear accepted. Comparable seller grades range from Very Good to Excellent.

**1966 To 1971 Large-Guard Standard:** Original cherry or later walnut finish, pickups and principal hardware, original case, no disclosed structural repair. Normal light wear; a replacement nut can be present.

**1972 To 1979 SG Standard:** Cherry or faded cherry, original finish and pickups, original case, no disclosed structural break. Played to excellent; replacement strap buttons accepted. Non-cherry finishes excluded.

### How These Ranges Were Built

I checked Reverb Price Guide final prices against the linked instrument descriptions and used Heritage realized results where available. The records span 2023 to 2026, with at least three records per researched era group. Shipping and tax are excluded; auction totals include the buyer's premium. These are sale references, not dealer buying offers.

[IMAGE 1]

## Early Standards: Pickups And The Factory Vibrato

The early Standard combines two humbuckers, a bound rosewood fingerboard, trapezoid inlays and an ABR-1 bridge. Its small pickguard leaves the pickups in separate mounting rings. On a collector example, those original parts and an unbroken neck belong together.

PAF means Patent Applied For, the wording on early Gibson pickup decals. PAF and Patent Number examples overlap in the first SG years, so the early band covers more than one pickup combination. It doesn't assign every 1961 or 1962 guitar the same premium merely for its date.

[IMAGE 2]

The sideways vibrato is a distinctive part of the earliest Standard. Some players prefer the later spring-style lyre Vibrola, but replacing one system with another can leave a guitar with changed parts and extra holes. A complete original sideways assembly still belongs with the guitar even if its owner uses the arm sparingly.

### The Long Lyre Vibrola

Around 1963 the long Maestro assembly with the engraved lyre cover becomes familiar on the Standard. Its cover, arm and mounting hardware form one factory package. A missing arm is a different issue from a drilled stopbar conversion or an altered top.

[IMAGE 4]

The 1965 band uses cherry small-guard guitars with their original cases. Nut widths and nickel-to-chrome hardware change around this period. That's a narrower comparison than the early range, which includes more pickup and vibrato variation.

## Large Guards And Later Finishes

[IMAGE 3]

The batwing guard surrounds the pickups and supports them through the guard. It appears during 1966, with early small-guard guitars still requiring the earlier configuration considered. The later look usually includes the long lyre Vibrola and eventually taller witch-hat knobs.

The $5,000 to $8,000 research envelope includes original cherry and a later walnut guitar. It therefore doesn't establish a cherry-only floor or a separate walnut discount. The guard, finish, pickup set and repairs decide where an individual Standard sits inside that broad group.

Later Patent Number and T-Top humbuckers are part of the correct period specification. T-Top refers to a molded marking on the pickup bobbin, not a promise that the exterior decal alone can date it. An original later pickup pair shouldn't be valued as though it were a pair of early PAFs.

## The Returning 1970s Standard

The SG Deluxe briefly takes the Standard's place during the early 1970s. When the Standard returns in 1972, it has a small guard again, with smaller block inlays and later construction. The broad rectangular bridge is often called a harmonica bridge.

The $2,400 to $3,000 band is based on cherry or faded-cherry guitars with original pickups and cases. Non-cherry finishes are excluded from that specific band. Walnut, natural, tobacco sunburst and white shouldn't be called aftermarket colors simply because the table prices cherry.

### Color Outside The Cherry Band

[IMAGE 5]

Factory color can change who is looking for a Standard and what they will pay for it. A rare original finish is also a different market from a later respray in the same color. The [SG family comparison guide](/post/vintage-gibson-sg-family-guide/) supplies the broader model and finish context.

The present research doesn't provide a supported dollar premium for each non-cherry finish. I keep those guitars outside the standard cherry table rather than turning one attractive color photograph into a price estimate.

## Repairs, Original Parts And Value

An unbroken neck, original finish and factory pickups are the baseline for a collector SG Standard. A repaired headstock, a full refinish and a missing pickup change different parts of that package. Normal playing wear and a good refret deserve a separate assessment from structural damage.

For scale, the site's [published Les Paul condition benchmarks](/vintage-gibson-les-paul-market-value-guide/) give the following deductions. They're Les Paul figures, not measured SG Standard discounts; I use matching SG Standard sales to price the actual repair or alteration.

| Published Les Paul Benchmark | Deduction From A Comparable Original |
| --- | --- |
| Repaired Headstock | Roughly 40 To 50% |
| Refinished Body Or Neck | Roughly 40 To 50% |
| Pickup Swap Without Routing | Roughly 25% |
| P-90 To Humbucker Routing | Roughly 35 To 40% |
| Quality Refret | Often 5 To 10% |

These aren't deductions to add together. A guitar that's already priced as played, serviced or altered has some of those differences reflected in its starting range. A quality refret preserves an otherwise all-original guitar's classification while taking it out of the museum-quality category.


## Keep The Complete Standard Together

Original tuners, pickup covers, the vibrato arm and case can be difficult to replace with the right period parts. Keep removed originals even if the guitar currently wears replacements. A well-executed refret is maintenance; a reshaped neck is a more permanent change to what the buyer receives.

For the other models, the [SG value overview](/vintage-gibson-sg-value-guide/) puts Standard, Special, Junior and Custom side by side. For this guitar, send photographs and repair history through the [free guitar appraisal](/free-appraisal/) page. A retail reference and a dealer buying offer serve different purposes, with selling costs and margin included in the latter.

mainEntity.name: How Much Is A Vintage Gibson SG Standard Worth?

acceptedAnswer.text: Vintage Gibson SG Standard reference values run from $2,400 to $3,000 for typical 1970s cherry guitars to $13,500 to $25,000 for early small-guard examples, as of October 2026. Original humbuckers, the factory vibrato and an unbroken neck put the strongest examples near the top of their group.

mainEntity.name: Does A Small Guard Always Mean An Early SG Standard?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. Small guards return on the 1970s Standard alongside later neck construction, block inlays and different bridge configurations. A 1960s small guard and a 1970s small guard do not establish the same market category.

mainEntity.name: Does This Guide Price Walnut Standards?

acceptedAnswer.text: The later 1960s large-guard group includes cherry and walnut. The 1970s $2,400 to $3,000 band is cherry only; non-cherry catalog finishes are excluded from that band.

mainEntity.name: Does A Refinish Change Gibson SG Standard Value?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. The ranges assume the original finish described in each era's notes. A full refinish needs matching altered-guitar sales. Published Les Paul deductions provide context, but they are not measured Gibson SG Standard discounts.

mainEntity.name: How Can I Get My Gibson SG Standard Appraised?

acceptedAnswer.text: Send clear front and back photographs, both sides of the headstock, the pickups, bridge, case and any known repairs. Keep removed original parts with the instrument and include the history you know. Those details support an individual appraisal.
